screens.heading: You are safe here
screens.reassurance: This module will not post anything or create any accounts. You are just reading.
screens.goal: By the end of this module, you will understand how social media works, how to connect safely with family on Facebook, and how to recognise and block fake profiles and scams.

screens.heading: Patricia's story
body: Patricia, 71, of London, Ontario, joined Facebook to see real-time photos of her grandchildren in Calgary — first steps, birthday cakes, school concerts she would otherwise miss entirely.

One day a friend request arrived: a smiling man, a reasonable name, a few posts about Ontario. Patricia nearly accepted. Something made her pause. The account was three weeks old, had no mutual friends, and the photos looked like a magazine. A scam account.
Patricia pressed 'Delete Request' and felt proud. She had protected the connection she valued — without losing it.
screens.tellMeMore: The most popular social media platforms for Canadian seniors are Facebook (by far the most common), Instagram (photo-focused, popular with grandchildren), and YouTube (video content — not a social network in the traditional sense but a major source of entertainment and learning). This module focuses on Facebook because it is where most family connections happen.

screens.heading: Getting started on Facebook
body: Download the Facebook app from the App Store or Google Play, or visit facebook.com on your browser. Create a free account with your email address and a password. Add your name and a photo if you like.

Finding family: use the Search bar at the top. Type a family member's name. Look for their profile — mutual friends, photos you recognise — and tap 'Add Friend.' They will receive a request and can accept.
Your privacy settings control who can see your posts and photos. Tap your profile picture → Settings → Privacy → and set 'Who can see your future posts' to 'Friends' (not 'Public').
screens.tellMeMore: A Facebook Feed (also called your Home page) shows you posts from friends and pages you follow. Scroll down to see what is new. You do not have to post anything to use Facebook — many people only use it to read and look at family photos. Like a post by tapping the thumbs-up button. Leave a comment by tapping 'Comment.' Both take less than ten seconds.

screens.heading: Recognising fake profiles and scams
body: Warning signs of a fake account: created recently (check by looking at posts — how far back do they go?), few or no mutual friends, profile photos that look too perfect or are stock photos, sends a friend request out of nowhere.

Common Facebook scams: romance scams (a 'widower' or 'widow' becomes your online friend, eventually asks for money), fake prize announcements ('You have won! Click here'), urgent messages from a 'hacked' friend's account.
The rule: never send money to anyone you have only met online, no matter how long you have been talking or how real they seem. Real relationships do not begin with financial requests.
screens.tellMeMore: If you suspect a profile is fake: tap the three dots on their profile and select 'Find support or report.' Facebook reviews reports and removes fake accounts. If you have accidentally sent money to a scammer, contact your bank immediately and report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501 or antifraudcentre.ca.

screens.heading: Sharing photos safely
body: Before posting a photo, think: would I be comfortable if anyone saw this? With your privacy set to 'Friends,' only people you have personally accepted can see your posts.
For maximum safety with grandchildren's photos: post to a private Facebook Group that only family members belong to. This keeps children's faces off the public internet entirely.
You can also send photos privately through Facebook Messenger — tap the paper airplane icon to send directly to one person, invisible to everyone else.
screens.tellMeMore: Once a photo is posted publicly on the internet, it is very difficult to control who saves or shares it. This is especially important for photos of grandchildren. Private groups and direct messages are the safest way to share family photos. Ask your grandchildren's parents what they are comfortable with before posting photos of their children.

screens.heading: Social media connects family — on your terms
takeaways: Set your Facebook privacy to 'Friends' immediately after creating an account.
Fake profile warning signs: recently created, no mutual friends, perfect photos, sent a request out of nowhere.
Never send money to anyone you have only met online.
Report fake accounts using the three-dot menu on their profile.
For the most private family photo sharing, use a private Facebook Group or direct Messenger.
screens.confidence: You can now connect with family on social media, share photos safely, and confidently spot and block the scams designed to take advantage of people on these platforms.
